criteria.criterion: The rendered page's title, heading and opening paragraph name Athena, say what Athena is, and say who made the study and why, before firstmate is discussed.
criteria.evidence: site.rs: title and h1 are now 'Athena explains how {sys} handles work'. The first lede paragraph is intro.json about.athena ('Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change…'). The second is about.study, which says what a study is and that 'Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project…'. The test the_page_names_athena_before_firstmate_and_has_next_steps checks the order h1 < Athena text < study text < firstmate text.

criteria.criterion: The page says what firstmate is in plain words, including that its workers are AI coding agents, who would use it, and what problem it solves. The page also explains what a study is.
criteria.evidence: New first 'what' item in intro.json: 'Firstmate is a tool for people who direct AI coding agents… hands each one to a worker, which is itself an AI coding agent, so that several tasks can run side by side without the workers overwriting each other's files…'. about.study defines a study. One caveat about claim support is in the findings.

criteria.criterion: The pinned repository URL is an HTML link, and each claim source is a link to the pinned commit's file and lines when the repository is on GitHub. The link text is HTML-escaped.
criteria.evidence: repo_link renders as escape(repo). Each claim source renders as escape(text), giving blob//#Lstart-Lend. The test a_github_pin_gives_linked_repository_and_sources_and_others_do_not checks both the linked case and the plain-text case for non-GitHub repositories. The real pin (https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate.git) matches github_base.

findings.summary: The new firstmate definition says more than the claims it cites support
findings.evidence: The sentence says workers are AI coding agents, that firstmate is for people who direct them, and that tasks run side by side without a person starting each agent. It cites c1, c11, c21 and c22. Those claims cover backlog moves, captain approval, harness choice and isolated worktrees. None says that workers are AI agents or that tasks run concurrently. The concurrency claim (the one at claims.json line 35, 'no concurrency cap') is not cited. Meanwhile, the page itself says every statement is traced to a claim. Citing the concurrency claim, or noting where the claims do not cover the sentence, would keep the page's traceability promise.

findings.summary: The captain gloss adds 'The person', which claim c11 does not state
findings.evidence: Claim c11 only says the captain approves merges when yolo is off. It does not say the captain is a person. The clearer wording meets the criterion but goes slightly beyond its cited claim.

findings.summary: A long line in the design doc was not rewrapped
findings.evidence: The line 'The text lives in `intro.json`… cites claim ids from `claims.json`; a' runs well past the doc's usual line width.

summary: The change fixes the problem where it starts, in the site generator and the intro data. The page title, heading and opening now name Athena and explain what a study is and why this one was made, all before firstmate appears. The firstmate definition now says its users direct AI coding agents and that the workers are such agents. The glossary moved after the main sections, and the captain entry is clearer. The repository and every claim source link to the pinned commit on GitHub, with the link text escaped. A new Next steps section links to Athena and to firstmate. Finding f2 is now in plain language. I ran cargo test --workspace and cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets, and both pass. The new xtask tests check the page order, the Athena-first opening and the links. cargo run -p xtask -- site succeeds. All changed files are on the expected deliverables list. There are two minor findings. First, the new firstmate definition says things its cited claims do not support (AI agents, concurrency), even though the page promises every statement is traced. Second, the captain gloss calls the captain a person, which the cited claim does not say. Neither one breaks a criterion.
